rv.q: Portraying an actress giving the audition of a lifetime, Ms. Arianda is giving the first must-see performance of the Broadway season, a bravura turn that burns so brightly you can almost feel the heat on your face.

With the commanding Ms. Arianda giving a performance of such intoxicating allure, “Venus in Fur” provides a seriously smart and very funny stage seminar on the destabilizing nature of sexual desire: vanilla-flavored, kink-festooned or anything in between.

David Ives’ "Venus in Fur" begins with an exasperated playwright-director complaining to his fiancee about his long day watching auditions. He’s had to see 35 incompetent actresses. Then the 36th comes barreling into the audition room many hours too late and proves more than he ever imagined.
Venus in Fur makes for an often captivating experience.
Even if the cat-and-mouse games of Ives' comedy with teeth become too attenuated, the players remain transfixing in Walter Bobbie's mostly vigorous production.
Once Vandas agenda becomes clearer, the play starts running in circles.
Arianda delivers the same quicksilver performance she gave Off Broadway, only this time she doesn’t have to carry the whole show by herself.
Sexual heat is the last thing you associate with Manhattan Theatre Club; there's more erotic thrill in its lounge brownies than most mainstage offerings.
Theater-goers may experience similar feelings of submission, happily under the spell of Arianda's mesmerizing performance.
Arianda remains the engine that drives this intermissionless thrill ride, revving on all cylinders as she progresses from desperate actor to imperious seductress to all-powerful goddess.
After a fantastic first hour, the story restates what's already been said.

Her ability to go from dumb to powerful (also on show last season in the Broadway revival of "Born Yesterday") is remarkable and her physicality here, from her Noo Yawk accent to crossing her legs like a longshoreman in a frilly dress, is thrilling.
Venus in Fur works hard to keep your interest, but it lacks the dramatic development to fully succeed.
Unfortunately, the need to act bigger diffuses the rawness and intensity of the Off Broadway production.
Rarely does a play of such genuine and palpable eroticism make its way to Broadway and this one may well leave you gasping.

cn.t: Critics praise Nina Arianda's incandescent, star-making performance in David Ives' smart, erotically charged two-hander, though some find the play itself repetitive and lacking dramatic development beyond its clever premise.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but still engaged
sg.ra: SeatPlan confirms the Mezzanine overhangs from row G back, so K-Q sit fully under. The room is small enough (Headout: 'one of Broadway's more intimate spaces') that rear orchestra remains engaged. Rows P and Q are accessibility-friendly (no aisle stairs per folliesbroadway). Legroom tightens beyond row O per SeatPlan.

Headout and SeatPlan both name AA-BB center as premier seats with 'clean, direct look at the stage' and elevation that improves the view. aviewfrommyseat user on Mezzanine L row A aisle reported 'lots of legroom' with only a thin safety bar as minor issue. Excellent rake across the mezzanine.

SeatPlan and Headout both emphasize that the mezzanine has 'excellent rake' keeping all rows elevated with clean sightlines; Headout says 'no truly bad seat in the house'.
